# spatInfer

<!-- badges: start -->

<!-- badges: end -->

Strong autocorrelation and directional trends mean that regressions using spatial observations are prone to return inflated t-statistics regardless of the validity of their identification procedure. The purpose of `spatInfer` is to estimate reliable results from regressions using spatial observations by implementing the diagnostic and regression procedures introduced by Conley and Kelly (2024). A simple workflow is used to carry out spatial noise placebo and synthetic outcome tests, and estimate regressions.

These are applied to three estimators: Bester-Conley-Hansen, Ibragimov-Mueller, and Mueller-Watson. If these very different procedures give similar results you can be reasonably confident that your results are reliable.

## Workflow.

`spatInfer` is based on a sequence of four steps.

1.  `optimal_basis()` gives the spatial basis to include in regressions.

2.  `placebo()` estimates treatment significance from spatial noise placebos with every estimator in one call, and selects the tuning parameter of each: the number of clusters for Bester-Conley-Hansen and Ibragimov-Mueller, and the bound on average correlation `avc` for Mueller-Watson (SCPC). `placebo_table()` displays the results in one table.

3.  `synth()` tests the null hypothesis that the outcome is trending spatial noise, and therefore independent of the treatment. `synth_table()` displays the results, and `combined_table()` shows the chosen row of each estimator with its placebo and synthetic outcome p values.

4.  `basis_regression()`, `im_regression()` and `scpc_regression()` estimate the regression with each procedure, and `regression_table()` and `regression_plot()` display them along with the original, uncorrected estimate.

The final regressions should use the same settings as the placebo tests. In particular, if the placebo used `k_medoids = FALSE` (Clara clusters, for large datasets), pass `k_medoids = FALSE` to the regression so that its clusters are the same. By default the synthetic outcome is generated by a quadratic in longitude and latitude; `xy_interaction = TRUE` adds their product.

## Instrumental variables.

Regressions with one endogenous treatment and one instrument, written as in fixest, `outcome ~ controls | treatment ~ instrument`, follow the same workflow with `iv_placebo()`, `iv_synth()` and `iv_combined_table()`, and then `iv_regression()`, `iv_im_regression()` and `iv_scpc_regression()`. These report 2SLS estimates and Anderson-Rubin tests, computed by the reduced form approach of Chernozhukov and Hansen (2008), with BCH, IM or SCPC inference, along with the first stage F statistic. Display the results with `iv_regression_table()` and `iv_regression_plot()`.

## Tutorial

A step by step tutorial for least squares regressions can be found [here](https://morganwkelly.github.io/spatInfer_tutor/), and one for instrumental variable regressions [here](https://morganwkelly.github.io/spatInfer_tutor/tutorial_iv.html).

## Installation

You can install the development version of spatInfer from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("morganwkelly/spatInfer")
```
